topicRows.html:

For a baby already cruising along furniture, the authors describe a stable push wagon the baby approaches, pulls up on, and pushes by their own choice.

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective The book’s push-wagon example For a baby already cruising along furniture, the authors describe a stable push wagon the baby approaches, pulls up on, and pushes by their own choice. In the everyday Your baby is cruising and choosing where to move next. Age, interest & context In the book: Main discussion: 9 to 12 months. Appendix: 10 to 12+ months. Monthly summary: once they can pull themselves up. Already cruising along furniture; approaches and pulls up independently; stable wagon resists tipping. The book’s ages are guides; this belongs here only while the described interest and movement fit your child. The main discussion waits for cruising to become more efficient. The baby chooses when to approach the wagon and use its handle; the adult does not place them in a supported standing position. The authors distinguish this push wagon from a seated baby walker. They emphasize a wagon that does not tip when the baby pulls up, and describe slowing its movement while the child is unsteady. The monthly summary says “once they can pull themselves up,” while the fuller passage adds cruising. The fuller readiness description remains part of this example. Back to the books The Montessori Baby Movement activities / 9 to 12 months / Gross-motor development Push wagon, self-initiated cruising and walking; full continuation PDF pp. 163–165 The Montessori Baby Month by month / Months 10 to 12; Activities list for babies / Wagon Pull-up wording and 10–12+ wagon row PDF pp. 293, 301 The Montessori Baby Introduction to activities Individual timing, material suitability, effort and frustration PDF pp. 119–122 Paraphrased for this companion. topicRows.html:

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Follow a ball down the ramps The authors describe a ball tracker with ramps to watch and a ball to retrieve. Their standing example requires a large, stable support, with a ball and parts suitable for mouthing. In the everyday Your baby watches a moving ball or wants to drop it and find it again. Age, interest & context In the book: Main discussion: 9 to 12 months. Appendix: from creeping, around 8 to 10+ months. Interest in following and retrieving the ball; standing version requires independent pull-up and controlled lowering with stable support. The book’s ages are guides; this belongs here only while the described interest and movement fit your child. In the body example, the baby pulls up, drops the ball, bends to retrieve it, and repeats. Watching the ball is also part of the interest. The appendix lists the activity from creeping, around 8 to 10+ months; it does not require every baby to use the standing version. The authors choose activities by the baby’s current movement and interest. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Exploring stairs with an adult The authors describe supervised stair exploration for a baby who is crawling and interested in climbing. Coming down may need more time and an adult’s modeling. In the everyday Your baby is trying to crawl up a step or another low change in level. Age, interest & context In the book: Main discussion: 9 to 12 months. Stair appendix: from creeping until walking well, around 8 or 9 months. Crawling and interest in climbing, with adult supervision and help learning descent. The book’s ages are guides; this belongs here only while the described interest and movement fit your child. They notice that going up can come before knowing how to get down. The monthly table describes showing backward descent. The appendix’s stair material is a separate example: low, wide steps and a railing at either end of a bridge, listed from creeping until walking well. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Exploring a material that changes shape The authors describe pressing and squeezing pliable materials in their 9–12-month section. For play dough, they describe stopping and trying later if the baby keeps eating it. In the everyday Your baby is using thumb and fingers to squeeze, press, or pull. Age, interest & context In the book: 9 to 12 months in the main discussion. Interest in changing material with the hands; continued eating of dough means the authors set it aside. The book’s ages are guides; this belongs here only while the described interest and movement fit your child. Their examples include play dough, tissue paper to tear, and squeezable bath toys, within their broader requirement for suitable materials and secure components. For dough, the authors describe showing a press on the table or a squeeze in the fist. If eating continues, they put the activity aside and try again after a few weeks. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Room for their own movement The authors favor awake movement that the baby initiates, with room to explore, help when needed, and no propping into sitting or standing before they can get there themselves. In the everyday Notice how your baby moves now, what catches their attention, and when effort becomes frustration. Age, interest & context In the book: The movement chapter groups examples at 3–6 and 6–9 months; later sections describe the same self-initiated movement through walking. The baby chooses their movements; no propping, and help remains available. The activity may continue while it fits your child’s interest and current skills; the source ages are guides. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Baby, PDF pp. 121–122, 160–161, 163–169. Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace. Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed. When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A small invitation A conversation with your baby Answer a sound, smile or gesture, then pause. Your baby’s next response can guide the conversation. Start by noticing Your baby is watching your face or experimenting with sounds. Age, interest & context In the book: Conversation appears at 3–6 months and continues through 9–12 and 12 months+. Signs are introduced in 3–6 prose, with 7–9 in the recap. Attention to a face, sounds or gestures; a response need not be a word. The activity may continue while it fits your child’s interest and current skills; the source ages are guides. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Baby, PDF pp. 136–137. Come where your baby can see your face. Say something, listen, and leave a little space for their sound or movement. You can echo a sound, smile back, or put a few words to what seems to interest them. Raspberries, bubbles and changes in volume are part of the vocal play the authors describe. There is no need to ask for a particular sound or word. For families who choose baby signs, the book suggests pairing a few familiar spoken words with signs, such as “milk” or “done.” Its age labels differ between sections; the authors’ wider guidance is to notice the baby’s response and interest. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective What their hands are finding out The authors describe grasping, turning and passing objects between hands as exploration. Their examples depend on objects and every component being suitable for mouthing. In the everyday Your baby is reaching for an object, turning it, or moving it from one hand to the other. Age, interest & context In the book: Grasping examples appear at 6–9 months and continue in the 9–12-month section. Interest in turning, transferring and investigating objects; suitability for mouthing remains necessary. The activity may continue while it fits your child’s interest and current skills; the source ages are guides. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Baby, PDF pp. 119, 121–122, 167–169. A familiar object can offer a new experience as a baby’s hand movements change. The book describes differences in texture, shape and weight, and a rotating drum that answers a hand movement with motion and sound. The authors also notice babies exploring the basket or container itself. They leave room for this interest, within the same limits on safe finishes, size and securely attached parts. Natural materials alone do not establish suitability. In the everyday Sitting leaves your baby’s hands free, and they are interested in choosing and examining objects. Age, interest & context In the book: Main basket example: 6–9-month section after independent sitting. Familiar-object appendix basket: 5 or 6+ months. Independent sitting for the seated discovery basket; simple familiar-object variant also allows lying. The activity may continue while it fits your child’s interest and current skills; the source ages are guides. Their examples include a small group of kitchen objects with different shapes or textures. The baby chooses what to examine; an occasional name can fit without interrupting every discovery. A separate appendix example uses two or three familiar toys in a soft basket while the baby lies or sits. That simpler choice is distinct from propping a baby to use a seated discovery basket. Watch what your baby returns to, and change the selection when interest or challenge changes. Start by noticing Your baby is choosing between objects or moving toward something they want. Age, interest & context In the book: No fixed age; the source distinguishes babies from children who begin walking and can collaborate in restoring materials. For a baby who is not yet walking and helping put materials back. The book suggests a low shelf or basket with a small selection, each object easy to notice. Materials that are too difficult, too easy or no longer interesting can rest out of sight for another time. At this stage, the adult restores the materials after play. A baby does not need to put one thing away before exploring another. In a shared room, the authors keep older children’s small parts where the baby cannot reach or open them, while leaving baby-suitable objects accessible. They also acknowledge feeding choices, difficulties and the support a family may need. In the everyday Your baby is feeding, and you notice their gaze, sounds or movements. Age, interest & context In the book: No ending age for connection through breast or bottle feeding; weaning is described separately as personal. Breast or bottle feeding is still part of this family’s care. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Baby, PDF pp. 192–193. Holding the baby, meeting their gaze and noticing their response are forms of connection in the book’s account. This possibility belongs to different primary caregivers and feeding arrangements. The authors acknowledge that some people choose not to breastfeed, that difficulties may call for specialist support, and that feeding not going as hoped can bring grief. The relationship is not limited to one way of offering milk. Their account pairs manageable food and the baby’s pace with choking precautions and learning first aid. In the everyday Your baby is showing interest in food and meals. Age, interest & context In the book: Six months and signs of readiness; the book describes food exploration from six months to one year. Interest in food and meals while early solid-food experiences are unfolding. They describe noticing a food’s smell and texture, hearing its name and seeing it prepared. Eating can bring language and purposeful hand use together. Their preference is for food the baby can manage with help suited to their coordination, rather than being hurried to an adult’s pace. The book’s practical food examples sit beside choking precautions and a recommendation to learn first aid. The authors’ earlier descriptions of food interest are not the same as their explicit six-month-plus-readiness condition for starting solids. Age, interest & context In the book: Responsive crying care begins from birth; the dedicated care section gives no upper age for responding or seeking help. The child is crying; care and comfort remain responsive while the adult seeks to understand. They describe acknowledging a cry and responding with presence or holding when needed. They also recognize how tiring this can be and the value of support for the adult. Make room for their feelings, including on days when you still need to go. In the everyday Your baby wants you close, or another trusted caregiver is taking over. Age, interest & context In the book: Around six to sixteen months for possible separation anxiety. A trusted caregiver is taking over or the child needs familiarity around a goodbye. The authors describe letting a new caregiver become familiar while you are present and using clear words when you leave and return. Their examples of separation anxiety span roughly six to sixteen months, with different responses from different babies. A familiar book or brief shared ritual can become part of goodbye. When there is time, the book makes room for an unhurried hug. When there is not, it describes acknowledging sadness and gently handing care over. They favor an honest goodbye over slipping away unnoticed. Familiarity does not promise a tear-free departure; the caregiver’s support matters too. If your baby seems to want to keep playing, you can explain that wish to the other child. In the everyday Two children want the same object. Age, interest & context In the book: The source discusses the first year and changes near twelve to sixteen months. Two children want the same object; notice the child’s actual wish to keep or release it. The authors notice that a young baby may happily move to something else, or may want to hold on. Respond to what is happening rather than requiring either reaction. When your baby reaches for another child’s object, the book models asking whether that child is finished. Waiting, watching or finding another object are possibilities while the turn continues. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective When a standing child resists lying down for a change For a child who already pulls up to standing and resists lying down, the authors describe a standing diaper change with the adult seated low. Their emphasis remains gentle, private care and participation. In the everyday Your child already pulls up and wants to stay standing when a diaper needs changing. Age, interest & context In the book: No numerical age is given; the diapering passage says once the baby is pulling up to standing. Already pulling up to standing and resisting lying down for a needed diaper change. In the home chapter, the adult sits on a low stool while the child stands for the change, if the space allows. The later diapering chapter connects this possibility with a child who may feel vulnerable when laid down. The adult still explains what is happening and provides the cleaning. For a bowel movement, the book’s example has the child lean forward with their hands on the side of the bathtub; the same passage describes front-to-back wiping. The authors keep other possibilities in view: a wish to finish playing, choose something or take more of a part. A standing change does not explain every protest. If necessary care still meets resistance, they describe acknowledging the child’s feelings and proceeding with gentle hands. topicRows.text: An everyday situation When your baby hits, bites, pushes or throws When a baby hits, bites, pushes or throws, the authors look for what the movement might communicate while keeping a kind, clear limit on hurting. The adult helps when feelings are too strong for words. ↗
topicRows.html:
An everyday situation

When your baby hits, bites, pushes or throws

When a baby hits, bites, pushes or throws, the authors look for what the movement might communicate while keeping a kind, clear limit on hurting. The adult helps when feelings are too strong for words.

↗

surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas An everyday situation When your baby hits, bites, pushes or throws When a baby hits, bites, pushes or throws, the authors look for what the movement might communicate while keeping a kind, clear limit on hurting. The adult helps when feelings are too strong for words. In the everyday Your baby is showing a strong preference through their movements, and someone or something may be hurt. Age, interest & context In the book: Some babies show strong preferences from birth; this particular changing-behavior discussion gives around nine to twelve months and looks ahead to toddler participation in repair. A baby communicates strong preferences through hitting, biting, pushing or throwing; the adult must keep people and surroundings safe. The book describes some babies showing stronger preferences around nine to twelve months. A hit might follow unwanted handling; a push might mean wanting to get past. A bite might come with hunger, upset or teething. These are questions to consider, not certain explanations. Throwing can be a different kind of exploration: the object may be too easy or difficult, or the baby may be interested in how it falls. The authors look for another way to explore that is not dangerous or disruptive. Their boundaries chapter gives a basket of suitable balls as one alternative to throwing an unsuitable object. The adult stops hurtful actions and can move with the baby away from the situation when needed. During intense crying, the authors use few words, offer a cuddle if wanted and stay nearby if touch is refused. After calm returns, they give a short explanation and model repair, such as offering a tissue to someone who was hurt or putting thrown things back. They describe babies watching this before taking more of a part as toddlers. For repeated situations, the book looks at what happened just before, including noise, crowding, a difficult transition or an activity’s fit. Adjusting those conditions is another way to help. They follow that interest and explicitly distinguish early awareness from using the toilet independently. In the everyday Your baby is becoming interested in the bathroom or in what happens during a diaper change. Age, interest & context In the book: The room chapter says around twelve months for some babies and much later for others; the monthly table places preparatory skills at ten to twelve months. Diapering distinguishes first-year awareness from independent toileting. Interest in the potty or bodily functions; the full passage follows the child’s actual interest. This is an early-awareness perspective. The ten-to-twelve-month table is not a deadline or an instruction to start before interest appears. They suggest familiar places for bathroom things and ordinary, matter-of-fact words for body parts, pee and poop. Their first-year diapering discussion presents this as learning about the body without shame. In the room-by-room passage, offering the potty during a change follows the baby’s interest. The authors emphasize that other children will be much older when this becomes relevant. The monthly overview mentions a potty, training pants and noticing patterns under ten to twelve months. That brief overview sits beside the fuller passage’s individual-interest condition; it does not establish an age by which a baby should use the potty. Observation can help you decide whether to make room, offer help, or change something nearby. Start by noticing When you are unsure what your child is interested in or how much help they need. Watch what your child reaches toward, returns to, or spends time exploring. Notice their expressions and sounds, and what happens around them. Try to describe these details before deciding what they mean. You can do this while you are already together. Written notes are one option; both books also make room for simply watching when your hands are full. Notice your own words and reactions, too. The books use observation to understand an individual child and respond to them, including stepping in when help or protection is needed. What’s underneath Start with what you can see, then consider what it might mean. The books describe useful surroundings that change with family life, without requiring a collection of special furniture or toys. In the everyday When setting up the home starts to feel like another large project. Look at what is helping and what is making everyday life harder. A useful change might make something easier to find, reduce repeated tidying, or give an interested child more room to take part. They describe asking for help when depleted, and seeking a doctor’s help for depression. In the everyday When looking after everyone else is leaving little room for you. The authors describe practical help as well as emotional company. A trusted friend, relative, partner if you have one, or another caregiver may be able to share some of the work. Paid help is one possibility when it is accessible. In The Montessori Baby, help can mean a meal or a household task so you can spend time with your baby. The authors suggest a visible list of useful jobs for visitors who want to help, especially when you are too tired to work out what to ask for. The Baby authors direct readers struggling with postpartum depression toward a doctor or trusted health professional. Davies also describes getting a doctor’s help when feeling depressed. These help-seeking passages sit alongside the books’ ordinary ideas for rest and support. What’s underneath Care for the adult is part of caring for the family. The authors suggest a visible list of useful jobs for visitors who want to help, especially when you are too tired to work out what to ask for. The Baby authors direct readers struggling with postpartum depression toward a doctor or trusted health professional. Davies also describes getting a doctor’s help when feeling depressed. These help-seeking passages sit alongside the books’ ordinary ideas for rest and support. What’s underneath Care for the adult is part of caring for the family. The pause makes room to notice the situation and choose a response; immediate danger is an exception. In the everyday When you notice a strong reaction rising in an ordinary moment. The Baby authors describe acknowledging a crying baby, noticing their need, and responding with presence or comfort as needed. Their pause is part of remaining responsive. Davies also describes pausing before reacting and expressly excludes immediate danger. Neither book’s counting examples need to become a fixed delay. Later, the books invite reflection on your own feelings, reactions, and needs. This is a way to understand what happened and what might help another time. Both books make room for mistakes and another attempt. In the everyday After you have lost patience or let someone down. Keep the focus on your own words or actions. Davies describes taking responsibility for losing her temper rather than blaming the child for it. The Baby authors include apology and naming what could have been said or done differently, even while caring for a baby. They also invite forgiveness and learning from mistakes. Repair can be part of how a family lives together. It does not depend on being a parent who gets every moment right. What’s underneath Taking responsibility and making amends can be part of everyday family life. Look together at the care, rest, company, and practical work that need room in the coming days. Start by noticing When family plans seem to leave someone’s needs out. If you share care, check how the other person is doing and what support would help. The Baby authors suggest a regular chance to discuss arrangements, what is working, and what needs adjusting. Davies describes planning around different needs, such as errands, rest, friendship, and a child’s wish to play. Her example looks for a workable combination rather than making the child’s enjoyment a reward for being good. The books recognize many forms of family and support. Leave room to hear the other person’s concern and to find a way forward together. In the everyday When you and another trusted caregiver want to talk about different approaches. It can help to agree on a time when you are both able to talk. Describe the situation and what matters to you, then listen to the other person’s perspective. Both books favor requests that leave room for another solution. You can share a small piece of information or an experience if the other person is interested. Agreement on the big priorities can coexist with different ways of playing, comforting, or enjoying time together. The books also value what caregivers bring: their interests, stories, culture, and companionship. Notice and appreciate the concrete ways they help. What’s underneath Shared priorities can leave room for different caring relationships. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective When parents live apart Both books recognize families whose parents live in different homes. Their preference for contact with both parents is explicitly qualified by the child’s safety. In the everyday For understanding the books’ perspective on separated family life. The Baby authors acknowledge that separation may not have been chosen and that staying together can be unhappy or dangerous. Davies describes the possibility of a workable arrangement, while making the child’s safety the first priority and excluding contact where there is a psychological or physical reason against it. Age, interest & context In the book: Vocabulary objects:12+ months; matching objects with cards:14+ months. The separate vocabulary-card row says 18+ months. Start with naming and exploring objects; matching follows interest, and similar pictures follow identical matches. Picture cards without matching objects are a later vocabulary example. Formal naming tests are for children over 3 in this book. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Davies groups vocabulary objects around a familiar theme. A photograph of the actual object can make the match clear; a similar but different picture is a later challenge once identical matching is familiar. Say the names and enjoy finding a match. If an object lands on a different picture, notice it without turning the moment into a test, and return to naming another time. The book reserves its formal naming test for children over 3. Picture cards on a familiar theme can also extend the words you share. Stay with your child when using small real or replica objects; the book’s small-part supervision condition still applies. A finished picture is not the aim. In the everyday A child who enjoys marks may become interested in a brush, chalk, or a larger surface. Age, interest & context In the book: Chalk: from 12 months. Easel paint: able to stand unaided. Watercolors: from 18 months in the caption and appendix. Interest in marks and the particular material, with adult supervision; easel work requires standing unaided. At this age, chalk and readiness-based easel painting are the earlier examples. The watercolor description is a later possibility from 18 months. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Her watercolor example begins with one color, a brush, a small water jar, paper on an underlay, and a spill cloth. The child explores wetting the brush, picking up paint, and moving it on paper. Chalk on a large board or sidewalk gives room for whole-arm movement and wiping with an eraser. For easel painting, her table specifies standing unaided, a short-handled chunky brush, and one color of thick paint in a cup. Davies suggests putting paint out for younger toddlers when an adult can supervise. As with drawing, she shows how to use a material and leaves the experiment to the child. These are shared, supervised explorations, with no model to copy. In the everyday Notice an interest in pressing shapes down or changing a material with the hands. Age, interest & context In the book: Clay/play dough: from 16 months in the caption, around 16–18+ months in the appendix. Gluing: around 18 months. Interest in pressing, rolling or changing a material with the hands, with supervision. The clay example can be relevant toward the later part of this band. Gluing is the separate later example, around 18 months. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Her gluing example uses paper shapes with a small pot of glue and brush, or a glue stick. The movement is to apply glue, turn the shape, and press it onto paper; the appendix uses a few large shapes. For clay or play dough, she describes flattening, rolling, making a ball, and trying simple tools. She also names kinetic sand as another material experience. Small parts and sharp tools require supervision. The activity is the experimenting. A child may repeat one movement and leave the rest for another time. A walk can make room for what your child notices. Start by noticing They may stop, point, listen, or return to a tiny detail. Age, interest & context In the book: No fixed age in the outdoor-noticing passage; it addresses toddlers. Interest in a detail, sound, movement or quiet moment outdoors. The child’s current movement guides the choice. In the everyday Notice which movements your child seeks and where the available space helps or gets in the way. Age, interest & context In the book: No one age for movement; the appendix’s named movement rows commonly say 14–16 months and retain differing readiness conditions. The movements the child already seeks guide the choice. Running, jumping, climbing and riding are different possibilities. This band does not imply that a child is ready for all of them. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14, 247–248. The activity chapter makes room for movement inside when space permits and outdoors. Its ball example favors outdoor space for rolling and kicking. The book’s longer equipment lists include climbing, sliding, balancing, and riding, with differing age and readiness descriptions. They are possibilities to understand in context, rather than a set of skills to complete at this age. Start by noticing Notice your child copying a wiping or sweeping movement or asking to join you. Age, interest & context In the book: Wiping spills:12–18 months in the chart; cleaning caption: from 12 months. Appendix dusting/sweeping:16–18+ months; table wiping: once a child can walk. Interest in copying wiping or cleaning and a tool the child can manage. A cloth and shared wiping are the earlier parts. Sweeping and dusting have later appendix labels and can wait for interest and manageable movement. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14, 64, 246. Keep the cloth or hand mitt where the task happens, with help ready. For an interested child, Davies also describes a manageable broom and dustpan, with a marked place to gather the dirt. The point is joining the work. It will often be slower and less thorough, and you can stop before either of you feels overwhelmed. Returning the cloth can be a shared last step. A familiar household task becomes something you share. Start by noticing Notice an interest in carrying clothes, filling the laundry basket, or looking for matching socks. Age, interest & context In the book: Putting dirty clothes in the basket:12–18 months in the chart. The T-shirt example is 18 months; sorting and hanging cloths are later examples. Interest in carrying one piece of clothing to the laundry basket. The early part here is carrying dirty clothing. Sorting socks and hanging cloths are described from 18 months, rather than expected throughout this band. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Davies gives the example of an 18-month-old carrying a T-shirt while the adult carries the trousers. Sorting socks or clothing by color can be another small part, when it interests your child. Her laundry examples also include hanging small wet cloths with pegs. That adds a different hand movement and needs supervision for small parts; it need not be added to a simple carrying turn. Try it together Offer one item to carry to the laundry basket. Carry your part alongside them. Leave another small part available if they want to continue. Her watering example requires steady walking; her flower example uses stems already cut to length. In the everyday Notice an interest in leaves, flowers, carrying a little water, or the work you do for a plant. Age, interest & context In the book: Watering:14+ months and walking steadily. Washing leaves: around 15–16+ months; dusting leaves:16–18+ months. Flower arranging:18+ months. Interest in plants; steady walking is explicit for the watering example. Plant care can begin with the supported earlier parts. Arranging cut flowers and the fuller gardening examples are later possibilities from 18 months. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Her watering row specifically includes steady walking. Leaf care is another possibility: she describes a small sponge or plant duster. She also includes growing vegetables in pots for homes without a garden. For flowers, the book uses stems already cut to length, small vases, a little jug and funnel, and a sponge for spills. Your child may be interested only in pouring or wiping at first; the complete arrangement can wait. Her gardening examples include planting and ongoing care. They are examples of shared work, with supervision for small parts and sharp tools, rather than a requirement to maintain a garden. The amount they want to do can change from day to day. In the everyday They may reach for their clothes, resist help, or ask you to do something they managed yesterday. Age, interest & context In the book: Assisted dressing and taking off socks:12–18 months in the chart; dressing/storage row:14+ months. Reaching for clothes, trying one part, resisting help, or wanting more help on a particular day. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14, 51, 247. Davies suggests easy openings and clothes that allow movement, with a limited choice of seasonally suitable things within reach. Elastic waists and a roomy neck opening are examples. Break dressing into small parts. You might put a shirt over their head and leave the sleeves for them to try, or hold the back of a shoe while they put a foot in. Offer a little help when they are becoming frustrated. When you must leave, acknowledge the wish to do it alone and explain that you will help finish. Davies keeps gentle handling and connection alongside the adult’s time boundary. Interest in the tissue or brush and in copying the adult’s movement. Nose wiping and blowing are not the same task. The invitation is a supported turn with a tissue or brush. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Davies suggests showing how you wipe your own nose, then offering the child a turn. A few tissues, a reachable mirror, and a place for used tissues support the routine. For hair, she pairs a brush with a mirror. Keep help available and show the movement slowly; your child does not need to manage the whole routine alone. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective A limit you can explain and keep Davies favors a few clear limits connected to safety and respectful life together. The adult can keep the limit while understanding the child’s disappointment. In the everyday You may notice a rule changing from one moment to the next, or realize a limit needs to be clearer. Age, interest & context In the book: No fixed age; limits are to fit the toddler’s age and ability. Safety, belongings, shared space or inconsistent rules need clear adult responsibility. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Her examples focus on protecting people, belongings, and shared spaces. A response stays connected to what happened, such as putting away a ball that continues to be thrown indoors and trying again later. Consistency leaves room for thought. Davies suggests revisiting house rules at a neutral time as children grow; if an adult changes their mind in the moment, they can acknowledge it. Her checklist asks whether the limit is clear, kind, reasonable, and suited to the child’s age and ability, and whether the child can help find a solution. An offered cuddle may help, or your child may push it away. Davies keeps the adult nearby and available when touch is unwelcome, with immediate action to stop harm. In the everyday Your household or caregivers may use more than one language. Age, interest & context In the book: The multilingual arrangements are not assigned a fixed age; the discussion addresses toddler families. Different people, places or times in the family use different languages. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. One example has adults speaking their own mother tongues with the child and an agreed language together. Another uses different languages in different settings. Age, interest & context In the book: No fixed age; the source explicitly describes adult modeling and shared return for young toddlers. Familiar favorites can be a good place to begin. In the everyday Your child may be exploring a familiar toy in a new way. Age, interest & context In the book: Home play has no fixed age; the separate pretend-play discussion says around 2½ years and later. Interest in familiar toys and open-ended exploration at home. At 12–18 months, the relevant idea is exploring familiar materials. The pretend scenarios described later are not an expectation now. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. At home, Davies makes room for imaginative scenes from daily life. In her separate creativity discussion, she describes pretend play as processing experience and places its beginning around 2½ years and later. Her home examples include blocks, farm animals, trains, and vehicles. These are possibilities within a varied collection, not a shopping list. Materials still need to fit the child using them, with supervision for small parts. If a child attends a Montessori classroom, she makes room at home for daily life, outdoors, creativity, and rest without duplicating all the school materials. Age, interest & context In the book: From 16 months in the caption;16–18+ months in the appendix. Interest in threading; size and thread thickness depend on the child’s ability. These are different material examples; choose a manageable challenge rather than trying to follow every variation. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective A turn to add and stir When you have time to bake together, Davies includes a young toddler in adding ingredients the adult has measured and stirring with a wooden spoon. The shared process can be one small part. In the everyday Your child may watch you mix or reach to join the movement. Age, interest & context In the book: From 12 months for adding adult-measured ingredients and mixing; helping measure is a later 2½+ appendix example. Interest in joining a small preparation movement, with the adult sharing and supervising the work. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. Her baking caption gives these forms of help from 12 months. The adult has already measured the ingredients; the child can help add them or take a turn mixing. For children under 2, she suggests keeping practical tasks to one or two steps and adding more only as they become manageable. The work will take longer, and you can stop before either of you feels overwhelmed. The appendix’s later baking row, from 2½ years, includes helping measure ingredients. That is a different part of baking. This early invitation stays with adding and stirring alongside an adult. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Talk about a recurring night need during the day Davies suggests returning to repeated nighttime requests at a calm daytime moment. The adult and child can think together about what might help, while keeping the child’s need for support in view. In the everyday The same request for a cuddle, drink, cover adjustment or familiar toy keeps coming up at night. Age, interest & context In the book: No fixed age for the conversation; the book addresses toddlers around 1–3 years and its problem-solving passage includes preverbal children. Recurring nighttime requests that can be considered at a neutral daytime moment. Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14. The conversation happens at a neutral time, when the family can notice what was difficult and consider an idea together. In her wider problem-solving approach, even a preverbal toddler can contribute through an action or gesture; the adult may supply most possibilities. This does not mean the child must manage the night alone. Davies’s sleep chapter keeps the help the child needs, rejects leaving a child to cry alone, and makes room for extra support during illness or teething. If continuing sleep difficulties affect the well-being of the child or family, Davies advises seeing a sleep specialist. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective A ring off, a ring on The books describe taking rings off a post before finding a way to put them back. The books offer both as possibilities, with adult supervision and help when wanted. In the everyday Your child may keep returning to taking a piece out or finding where it fits. Age, interest & context In the book: Baby’s illustrated grid says 9–12 months; both fuller appendix rows say 12+ months. Interest in removing or placing a piece, with manageable materials, adult supervision and help. Included as a perspective from the Baby grid. The appendix examples carry a later 12+ label; removing a piece can be enough. The peg-box example has six holes and a tray for the pegs the child removes. Taking pieces out can be worth repeating; an adult can help reset the material. A separate example has three cubes that fit onto one vertical dowel. The cubes may begin on the post or in a nearby basket. This is a different movement from fitting pegs into holes. The Baby illustrated activity grid places both in its 9–12 month group. The fuller Baby and Toddler appendix rows say 12+ months. These are the books’ different presentations, not a deadline to reconcile. Choose a manageable challenge and let interest guide how long it stays out. Small parts need supervision; a child does not have to place every piece to have explored the material. Age, interest & context In the book: Baby appendix: around 13+ months. Toddler photograph: from 16 months. The Baby chapter also discusses the movement among older-baby activities. Interest in turning a flat piece toward an opening; suitable materials, adult supervision and help. This band spans two differently labeled examples. Interest and manageable materials matter more than reaching either printed age. The Baby chapter mentions older babies manipulating a poker-chip-sized piece into a narrow slot. Its appendix lists the slotted box from around 13 months, with the box and a basket of pieces on a tray. The Toddler chapter likewise describes a coin slot as a more precise posting challenge. Its photographed example is labeled from 16 months. These examples have different age labels; neither is a date by which a child needs to do it. The Baby appendix’s optional latch adds another challenge when retrieving the pieces. A simple box can keep attention on the posting movement itself. Show a small movement if help is welcome, then leave time to try or pause. The books’ small-part activities need adult supervision. Their household examples are possibilities, not a requirement to make or buy a special set. Opening and closing can hold a child’s attention all by itself. The books describe a few different closures to explore, with an adult choosing and supervising the materials. In the everyday Your child may want another turn with a lid, clasp or turning key. Age, interest & context In the book: Opening-and-closing baskets: 12+ months. Separate locks and keys: around 13+. Baby’s furniture-key example has an earlier 10+ label. Interest in a particular opening movement, with adult help and supervision of the chosen materials. The basket and separate-key examples have their own labels within this band. The earlier furniture example is context, not an instruction to alter furniture. Both appendices describe a basket of two or three opening-and-closing objects from 12+ months. A box, tin or purse offers its own movement; there is no need to collect every type. Keys are a separate example. The Baby appendix describes a key in lockable furniture from 10+ months, while the separate lock-and-key baskets in both books begin around 13+ months. The Toddler chapter also describes lockboxes. Turning a key, releasing a clasp and lifting a lid are different problems for the hands. A slow demonstration or adult help can make one part accessible without requiring the child to manage every step. Stay with the child when materials have small parts. Repeat an interesting movement, simplify the choice, or leave it for another time. These book examples do not require a new collection or a homemade lock board.
